text.p: Spain's opposition Socialists accused the new conservative government on Saturday of cheating in its draft 1997 budget so that Spain can join a European single currency and announced they would symbolically vote against it.
"This is the most trick-laden budget ever submitted to parliament," Jose Borrell, the top Socialist in the congressional budget committee, told a news conference.
The tough budget is already certain to go through parliament anyway on the votes of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's centre-right Popular Party (PP) and of its Catalan allies.

Former Socialist prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, who called and lost elections in March after parliament threw his own 1996 budget back in his face, is firmly committed to seeing Spain join the planned single currency.
But he and other Socialists had already warned that they might not go along with the conservatives' recipe for getting there.
Borrell said the Socialist executive committee would meet on Monday and ratify the decision to vote against the budget.

The 1997 accounts, designed to ensure Spain meets the tough criteria required for entry into the European Union's planned Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), are unsustainable, predicated on optimistic figures and impossible to fulfil, Borrell said.
His charges, aired amid rising tensions between Aznar's PP and the Socialists over a 1980s "dirty war" on Basque rebels, were rejected by the PP head of the Senate budget committee.
"It is paradoxical...that they should be talking about tricks and traps when they are the ones who used them throughout their years in government," Senator Francisco Utrera said.

Independent economists say the budget sent to parliament by Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato last Monday is convincing and credible on paper, but that achieving it hinges on sufficient economic growth -- a point Borrell underscored.
Rato says the assumptions underlying the budget for revenues and expenditures are "absolutely realistic".
The draft foresees 1997 revenue growth of just under six percent, the rough equivalent of the economy's nominal growth. Gross domestic product growth is seen at a real three percent.
Spending growth will be capped at 1.7 percent, which represents an expenditure cut of nearly one percentage point given inflation forecasts of some 2.6 percent.

Borrell said that even if all the assumptions for 1997 were to be met, accounts for 1998 would not work because next year's figures were based on once-off revenues and no steps had been taken to trim structural causes of the budget deficit.
